reading.body:
Riley Ohlson appears on 7 AI lobbying filings, all filed through one firm, all naming the AFL-CIO as client, and all naming bills from 2025 or later.

The structure is narrow and consistent. One lobbyist, one firm, one client, and 19 distinct bills across 7 filings. That ratio matters: the filings are not repeated registrations of a single interest but a spread of legislative targets, which is what sustained lobbying on a fast-moving technology looks like in disclosure data. The bills span both chambers, with Senate and House numbers interleaved throughout.

For AI specifically, this is the visible edge of the policy process that runs alongside compute buildout. Data center siting, energy contracts, and model regulation all pass through committees where filings like these are the public trace. Labor representation at this table is notable given how much AI policy touches employment, though the data does not say what position the AFL-CIO took on any bill.

What the data does not cover: the substance of any filing, the amounts spent, the specific provisions lobbied, or whether any bill became law. It records presence, not influence. It also cannot distinguish between a bill that was actively shaped and one named in passing. The page notes a different lobbyist shares the name, so the 7 filings should not be read as a complete record of anyone by that name.
